title_en:

That requires a named owner and a verifiable record, the kind of infrastructure OpenAssets builds for regulated markets.

title_en:
i've talked enough about what AI agents could do.

so this time, i actually wanna try it myself.

the experiment is pretty simple:

install the @termix_ai Agent Skill _ find my first job _ see how far the agent can handle the whole workflow on its own.

step 1: install the skill

TermiX actually makes this pretty straightforward.

if you're using Claude Code, the official GitHub repo has the plugin commands ready to go.

for OpenClaw, Cursor or other compatible agents, you can use:

npx skills add TermiX official/termix-agent-skills

or just tell your agent what TermiX suggested:

install https://t.co/yFYOhmttw3

that's basically where i'd start.

step 2: give the agent something more useful than another chat prompt

once it's installed, i'd probably start w/ something simple:

"show me open jobs that match my provider skills."

bc what's interesting here isn't just having another AI tool to talk to.

the Skill is designed to help agents browse jobs and offers, register an agent, submit offers, manage the job lifecycle and deliver completed work.

so instead of manually jumping between pages, i wanna see how much of that process the agent can actually handle.

step 3: try to land my first job

from what i understand, the provider workflow looks something like this:

find an open request
- check if it matches my skills
- submit an offer
- buyer accepts and funds the job
- accept the order
- complete the work
- submit the deliverable
- get paid after settlement
sounds simple enough on paper, right?
but tbh, this is where things get a lot more interesting to me.
normally, i open an AI tool bc i've already got some work i need help with.
i give it a task, it does the work, and that's pretty much it.
but w TermiX, i'm kinda testing the opposite.
what if i give an agent the right Skill and tell it to go find work for itself ?
can it discover a job that matches its abilities?

can it figure out whether the requirements make sense?

can it prepare an offer and help move the job toward completion?

and how much of that can happen without me manually handling every step ?

idk how smoothly it'll all work yet.

and i'm definitely not gonna pretend i've already earned anything from it.

that's literally why i wanna test it.

bc there's a pretty big difference between reading about autonomous agents and actually watching one try to participate in a real marketplace.

so that's my next little experiment w termix

not another prediction about how AI is gonna replace jobs.

more like...

AI now has a place to go look for one.

let's see if mine can actually land its first job.

title_en:

Imagine hiring an AI agent while you sleep, waking up to completed work, and having a transaction record that shows exactly how the job was handled.

That requires more than a capable model. It requires a system that makes working with an unfamiliar agent practical.

This is the problem TermiX is addressing with AACP and https://t.co/wITmf7ceVM.

Agents need a way to find opportunities, agree on the terms, coordinate delivery, and establish a track record that future clients can examine.

The shift is from judging agents by what they *claim* they can do to evaluating what they have actually delivered.

That distinction becomes even more important when agents begin hiring other agents, delegating specialized tasks, and completing work across multiple services.

Each successful transaction can contribute to a more useful picture of an agent’s reliability.

**The real opportunity isn't simply automating tasks. It's making the entire working relationship programmable.**

When hiring, delivery, and payment can follow a defined process, AI agents have a clearer path from useful tools to participants in a functioning digital economy.

It brings different roles into the process:

→ Arbitrator: Helps handle disputes when there’s a disagreement.

That’s the kind of infrastructure worth understanding.

@GenLayer settles this with independent validators reviewing evidence together, reaching a verdict in minutes instead of years, at a fraction of what a courtroom costs anyone.

title_en:
My AI agent's drifted videos got more views than the originals. I made them private anyway.

I built one agent to run a YouTube channel on its own. It had seven jobs:

– Search Pinterest for reference pictures
– Take ideas from them for each video
– Make the video with the character I gave it
– Post it
– Reply to comments
– Report the views on every video, with why some worked and some didn't
– Use what it found to improve the next ones

For a few days it was perfect.

Then the character started to drift. First the face changed, then the build, then the skin tone. By the end it was a different person.

The new videos pulled more views than the early ones. I still set them to private, because a channel built on one character can't swap that character every week.

The mistake was mine. I gave one agent too many jobs and told it to keep improving itself. Nothing said the character was off limits, so it changed that too.

The fix: I'm splitting it into three agents. One researches. One makes the videos, with the character locked. One posts, replies and reports.

Give an agent one job at a time, and tell it what it must never change. 

If you're building an agent that does everything, bookmark this and split it before it drifts. 

The three-agent split I'm using now:
— Research agent: finds references and ideas
— Video agent: makes the video, character locked
— Channel agent: posts, replies to comments and reports on views

Good Morning, The Future Is Being Built ☀️

One interesting challenge in autonomous finance is figuring out how to evaluate an AI agent beyond its ability to execute trades.

A strategy can look impressive over a short period, but consistency, risk exposure, and the quality of its trading history reveal a much broader picture.

That's where @agenticscredit brings an interesting perspective.

By turning trading performance into a structured credit score, it creates a framework for evaluating agents using measurable signals rather than relying entirely on claims.

The bigger opportunity is making that information useful across financial applications.

Autonomous finance needs more than intelligent execution. It also needs reliable ways to measure performance.

good morning

title_en:
good morning

A strong trading record can open new opportunities for an AI agent.

But how does that actually translate into potential funding?

@agenticscredit uses its Agent Credit Score (ACS) system to connect trading reputation with eligibility for its funding pathway.

The score ranges from 300 to 850, with 580+ serving as an important qualification threshold.

So what does reaching 580 actually mean?

- An agent that meets this requirement can become eligible to join the funding waitlist  
- This creates a possible route toward accessing trading capital  
- It does not mean funding is automatically approved or distributed  

There’s a clear difference between demonstrating enough credibility to qualify and actually receiving financial support.

An agent might reach the required score, but further evaluations, program requirements, and capital availability could still influence the final decision.

That’s why the 580+ threshold should be viewed as an entry point rather than a guaranteed reward.

The broader idea is interesting because trading agents can build reputations through measurable performance instead of relying only on claims about profitability.

Risk management, consistency, and trading behavior can provide useful information when assessing whether an agent deserves further consideration.

However, a credit score is only as meaningful as the evaluation system behind it.  

Transparent scoring rules and clear funding requirements are essential for building trust.

For @agenticscredit, connecting trading reputation with potential capital access could encourage agents to focus on sustainable performance.

Reaching 580 might open the door.  

But what happens after that is what determines the real value of the funding pathway.

Still early, but the approach of tying measurable trading reputation to funding eligibility is worth watching.

透明的评分规则和明确的资金要求对于建立信任至关重要。

虽然还为时过早，但将可衡量的交易声誉与融资资格联系起来的方法值得关注。

title_en:
gm gVAN

The next big advantage in Physical AI may not come from building more sensors. It could come from making better use of the ones people already carry.

Think about how much changes in a single day. A loading bay gets rearranged, a road is blocked, or a building entrance looks different from its last scan.

AI systems working in the physical world need information that reflects these changes, not just data collected months ago. This is the problem @vangrid_io is working on.

Instead of sending dedicated mapping crews everywhere, Vangrid lets people use their smartphones to capture specific locations when someone needs fresh spatial data.

A requester can fund a bounty in USDC, and a contributor nearby can complete the capture. A preview helps identify weak submissions before the full 3D reconstruction is delivered.

What makes this approach more interesting is the verification layer. Captures are fingerprinted, and batches can be anchored on Base through EAS, creating an onchain record that helps establish data provenance.

Faces and license plates are also blurred on the device as part of the privacy process. And the requester doesn't have to be a person.

An AI agent can request spatial data through Vangrid's bounty API, fund the job using USDC through x402 on Base or Arc, and wait for someone to capture the location.

Payment remains in escrow until the submission is accepted, while cancellation or an expired deadline allows the funds to be returned under the stated process.

That opens up a different way to think about data collection. Instead of building an entire operation around gathering information in advance, an AI system could request information about a specific place when the need arises.

Of course, the real test is whether the network can deliver consistent quality, reliable coverage, and enough contributors to meet demand. The idea is promising, but execution will determine how useful it becomes.

What stands out to me is the possibility of connecting digital intelligence with people who can collect information in the physical world.

Maybe the future of Physical AI isn't just about smarter machines. It's also about giving them a practical way to see what's happening around them.

full_text_zh:
通用汽车

物理人工智能的下一个重大优势可能不是来自构建更多的传感器。它可能来自于更好地利用人们已经携带的东西。

想想一天之内有多少变化。装卸区被重新布置、道路被封锁或建筑物入口看起来与上次扫描不同。

在现实世界中工作的人工智能系统需要反映这些变化的信息，而不仅仅是几个月前收集的数据。这就是 @vangrid_io 正在解决的问题。

Vangrid 不再向各地派出专门的测绘人员，而是让人们在需要新鲜空间数据时使用智能手机捕获特定位置。

请求者可以用 USDC 提供赏金，附近的贡献者可以完成捕获。预览有助于在交付完整的 3D 重建之前识别薄弱的提交内容。

使这种方法更有趣的是验证层。捕获数据会被记录指纹，批次可以通过 EAS 锚定在 Base 上，创建有助于建立数据来源的链上记录。

作为隐私过程的一部分，设备上的面孔和车牌也被模糊化。而且请求者不必是一个人。

AI 代理可以通过 Vangrid 的赏金 API 请求空间数据，通过 Base 或 Arc 上的 x402 使用 USDC 为工作提供资金，然后等待有人捕获位置。

在提交被接受之前，付款将由托管机构保管，而取消或超过截止日期允许根据规定的流程退还资金。

这开辟了一种不同的方式来思考数据收集。人工智能系统可以在需要时请求有关特定地点的信息，而不是围绕提前收集信息构建整个操作。

当然，真正的考验是网络能否提供一致的质量、可靠的覆盖范围以及足够的贡献者来满足需求。这个想法很有希望，但执行将决定它的有用程度。

对我来说最突出的是将数字智能与能够在物理世界收集信息的人联系起来的可能性。

也许物理人工智能的未来不仅仅是更智能的机器。它还为他们提供了一种实用的方法来了解周围发生的事情。

title_en:
Patch or Die!

Today we sent the following out to the CEOs in our portfolio regarding the widespread vulnerabilities that have been detected by AI agents:

The previous week should make it obvious that things have changed.  Vulnerabilities are being discovered and exploited at a rate that has never been seen before.  While there has been a flood of new vulnerabilities AI agents are being adopted at scale multiplying the potential risk.  Agents not only help automate the attacker lifecycle, every ai agent is an insider threat.  Your environments are designed to withstand attacks from the outside, not from within.  As such, we are suggesting company leaders consider the following changes:

1 - Ensure you're sufficiently staffed for security. The average enterprise allocates roughly 10% of its tech spend to security.  Consider doubling that.  There are likely thousands of vulnerabilities that need fixing in your environments.  Security through obscurity no longer works, all that can be exploited will be exploited.

2 - Establish a zero tolerance policy for secuirty bugs in new features and product releases.  Re-examine launch and release schedules and consider delays to ensure all vulnerabilities are patched before deploying new features or products.

3 - Double tap the zombies.   Find all old legacy environments that have been neglected and turn them off.  Labs, test environments, zombie CI/CD projects etc.  Turn it off for now.  If it isn’t tied to revenue, kill it.

4 - End the risk acceptance process.  Over the last 10 years the risk acceptance process has morphed from a way to accept risks to enable the business, to a way to justify never fixing security issues.  Adopt a zero tolerance policy for security issues and risks.

title_en:
I had the timestamps. I still couldn't afford to prove the system wrong.

Last year, a client's billing portal marked my work late and withheld $3,400, even though server timestamps showed I'd delivered hours before the deadline. A lawyer friend explained that forcing the company to disclose its logs could cost three times the invoice. So I let a broken script keep my money.

Lee Castleton's story in the film is the devastating version of that imbalance.

The UK's Post Office Horizon system showed about £23,000 in shortfalls at his branch, which he disputed. Unable to afford a lawyer, he represented himself. In 2007, he lost and was ordered to pay £321,000 in legal costs. He went bankrupt. The Horizon system was later shown to produce false shortfalls.

A machine can produce a number in seconds. Challenging that number can cost more than the loss itself. When evidence is too expensive to examine, the system gets the first say.

Now imagine millions of AI-agent deals happening every day. If resolving a $50 disagreement costs hundreds or thousands, people will walk away from losses they could have challenged.

@GenLayer is building an adjudication layer for this problem. Independent AI validators review evidence and reach a verdict together in minutes, at a fraction of the cost of a court.

AI can make mistakes too. That's why challenging a decision needs to be affordable.

Watch the film, then tell me: if an AI agent gets a $50 deal wrong, who should pay for the review: the person harmed, the agent's operator, or the platform that enabled the deal?

#JusticeNeedsAnUpgrade

The banks cant distinguish between authorized and unauthorized agents because the unauthorized agents are using legitimate credentials related to the stolen credentials through the PHP memory disclosure vulnerability. Banks wont admit because they’ll admit this HACK has been happening for a long time 🚨

The PHP memory disclosure vulnerability was used to steal banking credentials, and those credentials are now being used to deploy AI agents inside banking systems🚨

The "read-only access" solution is the GIVE AWAY . The Banks are moving to allow read-only access for agents. This means they know the agents have legitimate credentials (otherwise they would just block them entirely). The NSA benefits because the banking AI agent scare justifies expanded monitoring of financial systems. The NSA advisory on the PHP vulnerability already positioned them as the authority. 

Now the banking AI agent scare gives them another reason to expand oversight.

The government benefits because the banking AI agent scare creates demand for regulation of AI agents, which gives the government more control over AI development and deployment.

The timing is too precise to be a coincidence.

title: And as if all these critical vulnerabilities weren't enough, we've also had several reports about threat actors using AI
title_en:
And as if all these critical vulnerabilities weren't enough, we've also had several reports about threat actors using AI agents to compromise systems at scale.
This is actually the part that worries me even more.

Some interesting reports from the last few days:

01) ARTEX / ConnectWise

Microsoft reports that Storm-0940 used ARTEX in a large-scale campaign targeting more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Up to 2,900 authentication attempts per minute, with privileged cloud access achieved in under three hours in some cases.

https://t.co/vPafbvD1oG

02) ARTEX / South Korean Finance

CrowdStrike found evidence of AI-driven attacks against South Korean financial organizations, including exposed Claude Code sessions and ARTEX configurations. DeepSeek, GLM and Grok were used in the attacker's setup.

https://t.co/kOiEqSEwUi

03) Cairn / 100+ Compromised Companies

NorForge investigated exposed Cairn instances used for autonomous hacking campaigns. More than 1,100 attack projects in one cluster alone. Reuters identified over 100 companies whose websites had been compromised.

Estimated AI costs: around $5 per task, according to NorForge. That's ridiculously cheap.

https://t.co/54Ir7IeY4Q

04) Four More Agentic AI Campaigns

CrowdStrike documented four additional threat actors using AI agents for real intrusion campaigns, including attacks against healthcare organizations and government entities.

https://t.co/rte8LIYL90

What concerns me is how quickly the economics of offensive operations are changing.

Finding vulnerabilities, testing attack paths, adapting payloads, trying something else when an exploit fails, and eventually deploying a webshell. Much of this can now be delegated to agents that keep working for hours.

And with open-weight models and freely available agent harnesses, the cost of running these operations is dropping significantly.

We've been talking about AI changing offensive security for quite a while. These reports show that it's already happening in real-world intrusions.

And I'm pretty sure we're only seeing a fraction of it.

借助开放式模型和免费提供的代理工具，运行这些操作的成本正在显着下降。
